GENERAL BOOTH'S
NEW RECRUIT.
His Granddaughter Enters Salvation Army Training Home.
SPARTAN RULES.

The Salvation Army has gained another earliest recruit in the person of General Booth's grandchildren. From to-day Miss Mary Booth, the second daughter of Mr. Bramwell Booth, chief of the staff, will be known as Cadet Mary Booth.

She is a shy and retiring young lady of twenty, and for some time past has lived at High Barnet with her family. She has many accomplishments, is a splendid violinist, and has a taste for modelling and sculpture.

To the Daily Mirror yesterday she said she had had no time to form an opinion as to what the training at the Salvation Army Home at Clapton was like. It was her first day, but she hoped to be able to do some good work for the army.

She had always hoped to do something for the betterment of the people, and desired to begin his first as the poorest probationer did.

The Daily Round.

"I have always felt drawn to the work of the army," she confessed, "and hope to be as good a soldier as those who have gone before. I am not striving for position as much as to do good to my fellow-creatures, and am prepared to undergo any training for that purpose."

The period of training extends over ten months, and is a most arduous time for the young probationer. Miss Booth will be quartered in the training home with the poorest aspirants to a position in the army.

The daily routine of a cadet in the Salvation Army is an exacting one. The time-table is as follows:—

11.15 to 12.0.—Bible class 12.15 to 12.45 p.m.—Verbal examination on the 1.0 to 1.45.—Dinner: two or three courses. 2.0 to 3.30.—Household duties, scrubbing floors, etc., and any personal requirements. 3.45 p.m.—Classes on army discipline, on the method of army duty. Theoretical and with object lessons.

4.45 p.m.-A plain tea.
5.15 p.m.-Prayers for field officers.
6.0 to 8.45.-Classes for shorthand and other educational subjects for the better equipment of the probationer.

9. 0 p.m.—Support for "Lights out."

On Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday afternoons the cadet is required to attend with a "company" one or other of the branches in the East End or the North-West. She has to start away about midday, with her "rations" in a little bag, has to walk to Limehouse, Walthamstow, Leyton, or wherever she is ordered, do house-to-house visiting, work with the local corps, and then walk back to the Clapton Congress Hall.

Friday afternoons she has free to do what she

likes.
"All this Miss Mary Booth is prepared for.
"I am so frightfully nervous of speaking," she remarked yesterday. "I am afraid I shall never get over it." But the Daily Mirror was assured that the young lady has already made her mark as a speaker, and that she has a winning manner on the platform.
